CH Series: High Speed Precision Engine Lathe # The CH Series is KINWA’s general-purpose high-speed precision engine lathe line. It is designed for stable manual turning, easy operation and long-term reliability in workshops, maintenance departments, tool rooms, mold shops, technical schools and high-mix low-volume production.
The series includes three models. CH-400 and CH-430 use spindles with 51 mm and 58 mm bore respectively, while CH-530 provides a larger 532 mm swing. Instead of a turret, the tools are mounted on a gang bed fixed to the cross slide. This arrangement shortens tool-change travel, reduces cycle time and keeps the machine footprint small.

Frequently Asked Questions # The questions below are based on KINWA’s official lathe knowledge guide. The answers are summarized for quick reading; the full answers are available on the official FAQ page.
What is a lathe? # A lathe is a machine tool that rotates a workpiece while a cutting tool removes material. It is used to machine cylindrical surfaces, faces, tapers, threads and other rotationally symmetric features. The workpiece is usually held in a chuck or other workholding device and rotated by the spindle while the tool moves to create the required size and shape.
What is turning? # Turning is a machining process in which a rotating workpiece is cut by a feeding cutting tool. A lathe is the primary machine used for turning. Common operations include external turning, facing, boring, taper turning, grooving, parting and thread cutting.
How does a lathe work? # The spindle rotates the workpiece to create the primary cutting motion, while the cutting tool feeds longitudinally, crosswise or at an angle. By controlling spindle speed, feed, depth of cut and tool position, the required dimensions and geometry are produced.
What is a manual lathe? # A manual lathe, also called a conventional lathe, is a lathe in which the operator directly controls tool position, feed and the machining process. It is suited to one-off parts, high-mix low-volume work, repair, fitting and jobs that require frequent on-the-spot adjustment.
What is a CNC lathe? # A CNC lathe is controlled by a computer numerical control system. The control executes a machining program to manage spindle operation, tool position, feed movement and machining sequence. CNC lathes are commonly used for repetitive machining and production runs.
What shapes and parts can a lathe machine? # A lathe is mainly suited to workpieces with rotationally symmetric features: outside diameters, bores, faces, tapers, threads and grooves. Common examples include shafts, sleeves, bushings, rollers, flanges and fittings. Actual capability depends on workpiece size, material, workholding, tooling, accuracy requirements and machine configuration.
Why do metalworking shops need lathes? # Lathes support shafts, sleeves, repair parts and other rotational components. They provide flexibility for one-off, low-volume, repair and repeat production, and increase in-house machining capability. Shops that regularly process rotationally symmetric parts can reduce dependence on outside suppliers.
What is the main difference between manual and CNC lathes? # Both can perform outside turning, boring, facing and threading. The main difference is control: a manual lathe relies on the operator to position the tool and control the process in real time, while a CNC lathe executes a program and predefined cutting conditions. Manual lathes offer flexibility; CNC lathes offer repeatability and production efficiency.
Are manual lathes still worth buying? # Yes, in the right production environment. Manual lathes remain practical for one-off parts, low-volume work, repair, prototyping and jobs requiring direct shop-floor adjustment. The decision should be based on workpiece type, production volume, operator capability and workflow, not on automation level alone.
Can a manual lathe perform precision machining? # Yes. Achievable accuracy depends on machine condition, tooling and workholding, cutting conditions, measurement methods and operator skill. A manual lathe should not automatically be considered a low-accuracy machine, but its actual capability must be evaluated for the specific part and tolerance.

From One Lathe in 1968 to a Global Lathe Brand # KINWA’s history is closely tied to the development of Taiwan’s machine tool industry. The company began as a small machining business and grew into a lathe manufacturer with decades of export and OEM experience.

In 1973 the company began manufacturing lathes under the name CHIN HO Machinery Factory. In 1980 it moved to Daya District, Taichung City, and was reorganized as CHIN HUNG MACHINERY CO.,LTD.
The company’s product focus has remained on lathes. Its manual lathe range includes high-speed precision lathes, heavy-duty precision lathes and large heavy-duty lathes. Its CNC range includes gang-type, slant-bed and flat-bed lathes. KINWA states that the goal is not to offer the machine with the most specifications, but to help customers select the lathe best suited to their actual machining conditions.

Oil and Gas Pipeline Components # Oil and gas equipment includes flanges, valve bodies, pipe fittings, connectors, adapters and long shafts that often require large diameters, large spindle bores and long between-centers capacity. KINWA lists oil and gas pipelines as one of the main applications for its lathes.
For this work, the most relevant KINWA models are the large flat-bed CNC lathes and the CHK heavy-duty manual lathes. The flat-bed CL-58, CL-68 and CL-78 offer spindle bores from 120 mm to 530 mm and between-centers lengths up to 7,200 mm. The CHK-860 and CHK-1020 offer Ø860–Ø1020 mm swing and 105/153 mm spindle bore for manual machining of large parts.

Lathe Products for Different Machining Requirements # KINWA builds both manual lathes and CNC lathes in Taiwan. The range covers small high-speed lathes, heavy-duty lathes, large lathes for long shafts, compact gang-type CNC lathes, slant-bed CNC lathes and flat-bed CNC lathes with large spindle bores.
The product pages below are organized by series. Each series page lists the available models and key specifications, with direct links to the corresponding official product page.
Specifications are subject to change without notice. Actual configuration, optional equipment and accuracy depend on the quotation and the workpiece requirements.
Manual lathes CNC lathes Manual Lathes # Manual lathes are operated directly by the operator and are suited to one-off parts, repair work, tool rooms, maintenance, education and high-mix low-volume production.
CH Series High Speed Precision Engine Lathe — Models CH-400, CH-430 and CH-530. Swing over bed 406–532 mm; spindle bore 51–78 mm; 5 HP main motor. A general-purpose high-speed lathe for workshops, maintenance and training. CHD Series Heavy Duty Precision Lathe — Models CHD-560, CHD-660 and CHD-760. Swing over bed 560–760 mm; spindle bore 86–104 mm; 10 HP main motor. For larger workpieces and heavier cutting. CHK Series Heavy Duty Precision Lathe — Models CHK-860 and CHK-1020. Swing over bed Ø860–Ø1020 mm; spindle bore 105/153 mm; between-centers lengths up to 8,500 mm. For large, long and heavy workpieces. CNC Lathes # CNC lathes use a control system and machining program to execute tool movements. They are suited to repeat production, stable accuracy and automated manufacturing.
CL Series - Gang Type — Models CL-10 and CL-100. Compact gang-type CNC lathes for small parts, polygonal turning and high-volume production. CL Series - Slant Bed — Models CL-220, CL-250, CL-280 and CL-320. Slant-bed CNC lathes with 8–15 inch chucks, bar capacity up to 115 mm and optional driven tooling. CL Series - Flat Bed — Models CL-650, CL-38, CL-58, CL-68 and CL-78. Flat-bed CNC lathes with swing up to 1,500 mm, spindle bores up to 530 mm and long between-centers capacities. How to Choose a KINWA Lathe # KINWA recommends evaluating the following factors before selecting a model:
Workpiece material, maximum diameter and maximum length Required dimensional accuracy and surface finish Workpiece weight and cutting load General cutting or heavy-duty cutting One-off, high-mix low-volume or mass production Manual operation or CNC control Required spindle bore, spindle speed, horsepower and torque Tooling configuration, optional accessories and factory space Contact KINWA for model selection · Download catalogs
